processing: Accounts describe tea made from the leaves of a wild Himalayan plant, and one describes it as a brick tea. The details of its manufacture are not recorded in any depth.
harvest_season: Not recorded for this tea. Himalayan gardens in general pick from spring into autumn, with a winter pause.
appearance_dry: Not reliably described; older accounts mention a brick form, which would mean a dark compressed leaf.
appearance_liquor: Not reliably described; a clear amber is a reasonable expectation for a mellow Himalayan black tea.
taste_profile: Remembered as smooth and mellow, with subtle floral and fruity notes.

brewing.notes: No traditional method is recorded. This is a general starting point for a mellow Himalayan black tea; taste at three minutes and adjust.

vintage_note: There is no established way this tea is sold by year or season, and the original estate trade ended after 1964. Tea from the wider district is now associated with the Chaukori gardens. Treat anything labelled Berinag as a modern regional tea and ask the seller for the garden and picking date.
description:
Berinag is a hill town in eastern Uttarakhand, and its name is better known today as a memory than as a product. The tea from its estate is remembered as a favourite of London tea houses.

Accounts say it was made from the leaves of a wild plant growing across the Himalayas, and that the trade name goes back to a Chinese variety. One describes it as a brick tea. How these details fit together is unclear, so take them as tradition rather than a recipe.

The flavour it is remembered for is smooth and mellow, with light floral and fruity notes. Without a documented brewing method, treat it as you would another gentle Himalayan black tea: slightly off-boiling water and a moderate steep.

Today growing is reported only around Chaukori, known for gardens the British established. If you see the Berinag name on a packet, ask which garden made it, because the old estate no longer runs as it did.
history:
The Berinag estate was bought from Kedar Dutt Pant by Thakur Dan Singh Bist (also spelled Bisht), and the tea was distributed by his company, D.S. Bist & Sons. He promoted it until his death in 1964, with markets said to include China, India and London. The start of that period is given inconsistently, so no firm date can be offered for it.

The architect Laurie Baker was a well-known admirer, and the writer William McKay Aitken is also linked to its reputation. After 1964 the estate is said to have been taken over by settlers and encroachers.
